claims.text: Under rapid heating and cooling, crystal-structure formation in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed primarily by kinetic effects.
Rapid reduction of noble-metal precursors causes fast nucleation of an FCC phase.
An early FCC template kinetically incorporates or traps subsequently available elements.
Slower cooling provides enough atomic diffusion for slowly reducing or thermally stable elements to segregate or form secondary phases.
A homogeneous, near-equiatomic precursor containing more than five noble and non-noble metals forms a single-phase FCC solid solution under rapid thermal processing.
The relevant precursor-reduction regime is approximately 150–250 °C.
Rapid nucleation produces an FCC solid solution with high defect density and lattice strain that can preferentially incorporate later-available elements.
The strained and defective FCC structure is a kinetically frozen metastable state.
Slower cooling increases atomic mobility, relieves lattice strain, and permits atomic rearrangement and phase separation.
Differences in atomic size and chemical affinity promote segregation or formation of additional phases once diffusion becomes sufficient.
Slower cooling or an isothermal hold will increase elemental segregation and multiphase formation relative to a rapid-cooling baseline.
Secondary phases produced under the intervention may include BCC or intermetallic phases.
The cooling-rate effect requires a significant disparity between noble-metal reduction or nucleation and diffusion of non-noble components.
The cooling-rate effect will be diminished when constituent elements have similar reduction behavior or when the composition minimizes lattice distortion.

contradictions.description: The mechanism describes rapid heating as causing simultaneous precursor reduction, but the proposed template mechanism and stated boundary require a substantial temporal or kinetic disparity in which noble metals reduce or nucleate before the other components.
